title: Why Freedom Is A Powerful Classroom Management Strategy agement-strategy/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin challenges the assumption that effective classroom management requires constant teacher control, arguing instead that over-management suffocates students and provokes more misbehavior, not less. He uses the metaphor of a large square: its boundary lines represent the rules and consequences a teacher must firmly protect, while the interior represents the freedom students need to learn and explore without interference. He offers guidelines for staying "outside the square" - leaving students alone once instructions are given, fading into the background as students work, occasionally joining an activity as a participant rather than an authority figure, and never using the 'listen and follow directions' rule to dictate how students think or learn. The piece frames restraint, not intervention, as the true mark of skilled classroom management.
points: Distinguish firmly enforcing rules (the boundary) from micromanaging how students work inside them.
Once instructions are given, step back and let students work without running commentary.
Fade into the background when students are on task rather than hovering over them.
Occasionally join students in an activity as a participant, not as an overseer.
Never use the 'listen and follow directions' rule to dictate learning style or process - only behavior.
quotes: But the notion that the more you manage your classroom the better is a myth. In fact, over-management causes more misbehavior than it dissuades.
Think of your classroom management plan as a large square. The four sides of the square mark one continuous boundary line.
The problem arises when you step inside the square and micromanage, throwing a wet blanket over inspired learning.
Allow them to wrestle with the academic conundrums you’ve placed before them without your interruptions and running feedback.
Many teachers misunderstand the ‘Listen and follow directions’ rule. It should never be used to dictate how students learn.
Teach great lessons. Give clear instructions. Protect your boundary line without surrender. And then get out of their way.
